# Statistical Models {#sec-modeling}


Predictive modeling uses information available at a defined time to estimate
an outcome that is not yet known. This chapter asks whether fields available
when an illegal-parking request is created can help identify requests that
close in under one hour. The model includes request detail, borough, grouped
creation time, business-day status, and area context from the Census-linked
table:


- population density;
- household vehicle availability; and
- median household income.


Request timing uses four six-hour groups and classifies Labor Day and the
weekend as non-business days. The remaining four dates are business days.


The analysis uses the same one-week, request-level data as earlier chapters.
It predicts recorded closure time; it does not show that request timing or
area characteristics cause a request to take longer or establish how
predictions would perform in a different week.


The under-one-hour target is a modeling choice, not a documented agency
response standard. In the 12,975 eligible requests, 4,478 (34.5%) closed in
under an hour and 8,497 (65.5%) took at least an hour. Recorded closure time
is only a proxy for handling time: it may include dispatch, travel, queueing,
reporting, and administrative steps. The analysis can predict this recorded
outcome from observed fields, but it cannot isolate those processes.


## Frame the Prediction


Before fitting a model, specify what it will predict and what information it
can use:


- **Unit:** one illegal-parking request from the distributed week.
- **Target:** one if recorded closure time is under one hour, and zero
  otherwise. Requests without a closure time cannot be labeled and are
  excluded.
- **Prediction time:** request creation. Closure time and later processing
  fields are unavailable then and must not be predictors.
- **Request features:** problem detail and borough, recorded when the request
  is created, plus its six-hour creation-time group and whether the date is a
  business or non-business day.
- **Area features:** population density, median household income, and the
  estimated share of households with a vehicle, linked through the ZIP label
  [@census2024gazetteer; @census2024vehicles].


The density measure divides ACS population by 2024 Gazetteer ZCTA land area;
the vehicle share is one minus the estimated fraction of households with no
vehicle. These describe area context, not curb capacity or individual
behavior. The ACS estimates cover 2020–2024, precede the request week, and
have sampling uncertainty. We do not calculate the vehicle share's
uncertainty from the published margins of error.


The ZIP label links a request to a ZIP Code Tabulation Area (ZCTA), but the
two geographies are related rather than identical, so this is an approximate
match [@census2023zip; @census2026american]. ZIP digits are labels, not
quantitative predictors. A later benchmark uses the ZIP as a category to
ask a different predictive question.


The prediction question is: among requests from this week, how well can the
recorded fields distinguish requests that close in under an hour? This is
prediction within the observed setting. It is not a question about
whether a predictor causes a longer closure, nor does it show performance in
a future week. The four checks in @sec-formulation-checks still apply: a
model cannot repair an unclear target, an invalid measurement, an inadequate
scope, or weak evidence.


## Establish a Baseline


A baseline sets a reference that a more complex model must improve. Because
34.5% of eligible requests close in under an hour, predicting the majority
class for every request already gives roughly 65.5% accuracy. That result
does not distinguish requests: it labels every case as taking at least an
hour. Accuracy alone would therefore make a useless classifier look
respectable.


The analysis starts from `load_parking_requests()` rather than
repeating the import and filtering workflow from @sec-wrangling. It links
the requests to the Census context already documented in
@sec-zcta-context-merge. The preparation functions leave the source request
data and the Census lookup unchanged. The merge indicator identifies ZIP
labels with no matching ZCTA.


```{python}
from scripts.parking_requests import (
    attach_zcta_context,
    load_parking_requests,
    load_zcta_context,
)

import pandas as pd
from matplotlib_inline.backend_inline import set_matplotlib_formats
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

set_matplotlib_formats("svg")

parking = load_parking_requests()
with_context = attach_zcta_context(parking)
matched = with_context["_merge"].eq("both")
pd.Series({
    "requests in one-week extract": len(parking),
    "unmatched ZIP labels": int((~matched).sum()),
})
```


The ZIP-to-ZCTA link matches 13,033 of 13,040 requests. For a complete-case
model, each matched request also needs all three area measures and the
request fields used below. The next check reports missing area context
and selects eligible requests.


```{python}
has_income = with_context["median_household_income"].notna()
area_features = [
    "population_density_per_sqmi",
    "median_household_income",
    "share_households_with_vehicle",
]
has_area_context = with_context[area_features].notna().all(axis=1)
eligible = matched & has_area_context
required = [
    "closure_hours", "created_at", "problem_detail", "borough",
    "incident_zip", *area_features,
]
model_data = with_context.loc[eligible, required + ["zcta"]].copy()
assert model_data[required].notna().all().all()
pd.Series({
    "matched requests without income estimate": int((matched & ~has_income).sum()),
    "matched requests missing an area measure": int(
        (matched & ~has_area_context).sum()
    ),
    "eligible requests": len(model_data),
    "matched ZCTAs represented": model_data["zcta"].nunique(),
})
```


Among matched requests, 58 lack at least one area measure, including nine
with no household vehicle estimate because their ACS household denominator
is zero. The resulting analysis has 12,975 requests from 176 ZCTAs. The
next step derives timing features from the creation timestamp. Four six-hour
intervals describe the hour, while the weekend and Labor Day form the three
non-business days in this week.


```{python}
model_data["hour_group"] = pd.cut(
    model_data["created_at"].dt.hour,
    bins=[-1, 5, 11, 17, 23],
    labels=["00:00–05:59", "06:00–11:59", "12:00–17:59", "18:00–23:59"],
)
labor_day = pd.Timestamp("2026-09-07").date()
nonbusiness_day = (
    model_data["created_at"].dt.dayofweek.ge(5)
    | model_data["created_at"].dt.date.eq(labor_day)
)
model_data["day_type"] = "Business day"
model_data.loc[nonbusiness_day, "day_type"] = "Non-business day"
model_data.groupby("day_type")["created_at"].apply(lambda x: x.dt.date.nunique())
```


The four other dates are business days. This distinction is descriptive
for one week, which contains only one holiday. The outcome marks closures
under one hour; closure time itself is excluded from the predictors. The
feature table keeps the ZIP label for a later categorical benchmark, while
the first model uses the other listed features.


```{python}
model_data["short_closure"] = model_data["closure_hours"].lt(1).astype("int8")
categorical_features = ["problem_detail", "borough", "hour_group", "day_type"]
numeric_features = area_features
feature_columns = categorical_features + numeric_features + ["incident_zip"]
X = model_data[feature_columns].copy()
X[categorical_features] = X[categorical_features].astype("string")
X["incident_zip"] = X["incident_zip"].astype("string")
y = model_data["short_closure"]
pd.Series({
    "under one hour": int(y.sum()),
    "at least one hour": int(y.eq(0).sum()),
})
```


The outcome has 4,478 requests under one hour and 8,497 at least one hour.
The train-test split reserves one quarter of complete requests for evaluation
and stratifies on this outcome to keep its proportion similar in both sets.


```{python}
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=2026, stratify=y
)

pd.Series({
    "training requests": len(X_train),
    "test requests": len(X_test),
    "training target proportion": y_train.mean(),
    "test target proportion": y_test.mean(),
})
```


The split contains 9,731 training requests and 3,244 test
requests, with nearly identical target proportions. Fixing the random seed
makes this example reproducible, while stratification controls only the
class proportions. Requests from the same ZCTA can appear
in both sets, so the test set evaluates new requests in areas represented
during training rather than transfer to unfamiliar areas. Requests from
each of the seven dates also appear in both sets, so the split does not test
generalization to a new day, holiday, or week.


## Use a GLM


Ordinary linear regression allows its fitted mean to take any real value
and typically models the remaining variation with a constant-variance
Gaussian distribution. A straight-line fit to a binary outcome can therefore
predict values outside zero and one, while the outcome's variance changes
with its probability. A straight-line fit to a count can predict negative
values, although counts cannot be negative; the spread of counts can also
change with their mean. These limitations motivate a model that keeps a
linear combination of predictors but uses a response distribution and link
suited to the outcome.


A generalized linear model (GLM) combines a response distribution from the
exponential family, a linear predictor, and a link function. The distribution
describes an outcome's conditional variation, while the link connects its
conditional mean to the linear predictor [@nelder1972generalized;
@mccullagh1989generalized].


For observation $i$, let $Y_i$ be the outcome, $\mathbf{x}_i$ its recorded
predictors, and $\mu_i = E(Y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i)$ its conditional mean. A
GLM relates that mean to $k$ predictor terms through


$$
g(\mu_i) = \eta_i
  = \beta_0 + \sum_{r=1}^{k} \beta_r x_{ir} + o_i,
$$

where $g$ is the link function, $\eta_i$ is the linear predictor,
$\beta_0$ is the intercept, $\beta_r$ is the coefficient for predictor
$x_{ir}$, and $o_i$ is an optional known offset whose coefficient is fixed
at one. Without an offset, $o_i=0$. A coefficient changes the linked mean
by $\beta_r$ for a one-unit predictor difference, holding the other
predictors fixed. Its effect on the original outcome scale depends on the
inverse link and the starting mean.


The exponential family includes the Gaussian, Bernoulli, and Poisson
distributions. For a continuous outcome, a Gaussian distribution with an
identity link gives ordinary linear regression. For an event indicator, a
Bernoulli distribution with a logit link gives logistic regression. For a
nonnegative count, a Poisson distribution with a log link gives Poisson
regression. These choices also imply different relationships between the
conditional mean and variance. The next two examples use the same GLM setup
but change the outcome, observational unit, distribution, and link.


### Logistic regression

For request $i$, let $Y_i=1$ indicate that closure takes under one hour,
and let $p_i = \Pr(Y_i=1 \mid \mathbf{x}_i)$. Because a Bernoulli outcome
has mean $\mu_i=p_i$, the logit link gives the following special case of
the GLM equation, with no offset:


$$
\log\!\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)
  = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_k x_{ik}.
$$


The inverse-logit transformation maps any real-valued linear predictor to
a probability between zero and one. Odds compare the probability of an event
with the probability it does not occur. For example, a probability of 0.75
corresponds to odds of $0.75/0.25=3$ to 1, while a probability of 0.5
corresponds to odds of 1 to 1. A coefficient describes a change in log odds,
holding the other included predictors fixed; exponentiating it gives an odds
ratio. An odds ratio is not a probability difference and does not by itself
describe a causal effect.


The first GLM includes problem detail, borough, creation-time group,
business-day status, population density, median household income, and
household vehicle availability. The three area measures are standardized
across training requests, so their odds ratios describe a one-standard-
deviation difference in the request-weighted feature values. The formula
interface compares each categorical level with a reference category and
holds the other predictors fixed. These coefficients describe
conditional associations in the fitted model, not changes caused by the
area characteristics. In the coefficient table, each categorical label names
the compared level; the level without a coefficient is the reference
category [@statsmodels2026generalized].


```{python}
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

glm_data = X_train.copy()
glm_data["short_closure"] = y_train
```


The training data pair each request's predictors with its binary outcome.
The formula below names the categorical predictors explicitly and
standardizes the continuous area measures. This produces a logistic GLM
with a binomial response and logit link. Requests in the same ZCTA share
area context and may have related outcomes, so the fit uses standard errors
clustered by ZCTA for its coefficient tests. Clustering changes the
uncertainty estimates, not the fitted coefficients or predictions.


```{python}
glm_formula = (
    "short_closure ~ C(problem_detail) + C(borough) + "
    "C(hour_group) + C(day_type) + "
    "standardize(population_density_per_sqmi) + "
    "standardize(median_household_income) + "
    "standardize(share_households_with_vehicle)"
)
glm_fit = smf.glm(
    glm_formula,
    data=glm_data,
    family=sm.families.Binomial(),
).fit(
    cov_type="cluster",
    cov_kwds={"groups": model_data.loc[glm_data.index, "zcta"]},
)
```


The fitted coefficients are on the log-odds scale. Exponentiating them
gives odds ratios, which make categorical contrasts and standardized
continuous effects easier to describe.

```{python}
glm_coefficients = pd.DataFrame({
    "log-odds coefficient": glm_fit.params,
    "odds ratio": np.exp(glm_fit.params),
})
glm_coefficients
```


For a continuous area measure, its displayed odds ratio compares requests
that differ by one training-set standard deviation, while the other model
features are held fixed. For a categorical term, the odds ratio compares
that level with the model's reference category. An odds ratio above one
indicates higher fitted odds of a closure under one hour for the stated
contrast; it does not say how many percentage points the probability rises.
The context values repeat across requests in the same ZCTA, so area patterns
are supported by 176 distinct ZCTAs, not by treating each request as an
independent area. These are conditional associations, not individual-level
effects or causal estimates. They also rely on a linear relationship between
each standardized area measure and log odds.


The coefficient table describes estimated effects but does not show how
uncertain they are. For the three standardized area measures, a 95% interval
for an odds ratio is obtained by exponentiating the corresponding coefficient
interval. The p-value tests a zero coefficient, or equivalently an odds ratio
of one, conditional on the other terms in this training-data model.


```{python}
area_terms = [f"standardize({name})" for name in numeric_features]
coefficient_intervals = glm_fit.conf_int().loc[area_terms]
area_inference = pd.DataFrame({
    "odds ratio": np.exp(glm_fit.params.loc[area_terms]),
    "95% lower": np.exp(coefficient_intervals[0]),
    "95% upper": np.exp(coefficient_intervals[1]),
    "p-value": glm_fit.pvalues.loc[area_terms],
})
area_inference.round(3)
```


The fitted odds of closing in under one hour are about 1.21 times as high
for a one-standard-deviation increase in median household income and about
0.81 times as high for the same increase in household vehicle availability,
with the other predictors fixed. Their intervals exclude one. The density
odds ratio is about 0.88, but its interval includes one, so this analysis
does not provide the same strength of evidence for a density association.
The interval widths and p-values reflect ZCTA-clustered standard errors;
they do not account for shared conditions across nearby ZCTAs or for a
different week.


Categorical predictors have several coefficients, one for each displayed
level relative to its reference. A joint Wald test asks whether all of a
predictor's coefficients are zero after accounting for the other terms.
The single-coefficient tests for area measures answer the same null
hypothesis one predictor at a time.


```{python}
term_tests = glm_fit.wald_test_terms(scalar=True).table.drop(index="Intercept")
term_tests = term_tests.rename(columns={
    "statistic": "Wald chi-square",
    "df_constraint": "degrees of freedom",
    "pvalue": "p-value",
})
term_tests.round(4)
```


At a 0.05 cutoff, problem detail and creation-time group have evidence of
conditional association with short closure, as do median household income
and household vehicle availability. Borough, business-day status, and
population density do not cross that cutoff in this fit. Failing to cross
it does not establish that their effects are zero. Nor does a small p-value
measure practical importance, improve held-out prediction by itself, or
establish causation. These tests describe the unpenalized training fit;
they are not p-values for the later regularized prediction model.


The evening hour group illustrates the distinction between a coefficient
and a term test. Its fitted odds ratio is about 1.23 relative to 00:00–05:59,
holding the other predictors fixed. The hour-group p-value of 0.0024 tests
all three nonreference hour coefficients together; it does not by itself
establish the significance of the evening contrast alone.


An odds ratio has a constant multiplicative interpretation on the odds
scale, but its probability-scale change depends on the starting probability.
For example, suppose an estimated odds ratio is 1.20 for a one-unit increase
in a predictor. The fitted odds are 20% higher, holding the other predictors
fixed. If the reference probability is 0.50, the corresponding probability
is $1.20/(1+1.20) \approx 0.545$, an increase of about 4.5 percentage
points. At a different reference probability, the probability change would
also differ. This example illustrates the conversion; it is not an estimate
from the request model. For a categorical predictor, the odds ratio compares
one level with the model's reference level. State that reference and the
predictor contrast whenever reporting a coefficient.


### Poisson regression

To demonstrate a count outcome, this example changes the observational unit
from requests to NYC ZCTAs. Let $Y_j$ be the number of recorded requests
matched to NYC ZCTA $j$ during the study week, and let $E_j$ denote its
population in thousands. Under the Poisson model, the conditional mean and
variance of $Y_j$ are $\mu_j$. With a log link and the known offset
$o_j=\log(E_j)$, the model with $k$ predictor terms is


$$
Y_j \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_j), \qquad
\log(\mu_j) = \log(E_j) + \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{j1} + \cdots + \beta_k x_{jk},
$$


where $\beta_0$ is the intercept, $\beta_r$ is the coefficient for
predictor $x_{jr}$, and $x_{jr}$ is predictor term $r$ for ZCTA $j$, for
$r=1,\ldots,k$. The symbol $k$ is the number of predictor terms. The offset
fixes the coefficient of $\log(E_j)$ at one, so the model
compares expected counts relative to population exposure. The request ZIP
labels are matched to ZCTAs by five-digit string, so the analysis uses
Census areas rather than asserting that ZIP Codes and ZCTAs have identical
boundaries. The code retains ZCTAs with zero requests by starting from the
full context lookup and joining the observed counts to it.


```{python}
zcta_request_counts = (
    with_context.loc[matched]
    .groupby("zcta", as_index=False)
    .agg(request_count=("request_id", "size"))
)
zcta_context = load_zcta_context()
poisson_data = zcta_context.merge(
    zcta_request_counts,
    on="zcta",
    how="left",
    validate="one_to_one",
)
poisson_data["request_count"] = (
    poisson_data["request_count"].fillna(0).astype("int64")
)
poisson_data["population_thousands"] = poisson_data["population"] / 1000
poisson_data = poisson_data.loc[
    poisson_data["population_thousands"].gt(0)
    & poisson_data["population_density_per_sqmi"].notna()
].copy()
pd.Series({
    "ZCTAs modeled": len(poisson_data),
    "ZCTAs with zero requests": poisson_data["request_count"].eq(0).sum(),
    "ZCTAs excluded for missing exposure or density": (
        len(zcta_context) - len(poisson_data)
    ),
    "matched requests represented": poisson_data["request_count"].sum(),
})
```

The left join keeps ZCTAs with no matched requests, which are valid zero
counts rather than missing outcomes. Areas without positive population or a
population-density estimate cannot enter this example and are excluded.
The model uses population in thousands as its exposure and standardizes
density so that its coefficient describes a one-standard-deviation contrast.

```{python}
poisson_fit = smf.glm(
    "request_count ~ standardize(population_density_per_sqmi)",
    data=poisson_data,
    family=sm.families.Poisson(),
    offset=np.log(poisson_data["population_thousands"]),
).fit()
pd.DataFrame({
    "coefficient": poisson_fit.params,
    "rate ratio": np.exp(poisson_fit.params),
})
```


The offset makes $\exp(\beta_1)$ a rate ratio: a one-unit increase in
$x_{j1}$ multiplies the expected number of requests per 1,000 residents by
that amount, holding the other predictors fixed. For example, if
$\beta_1=0.20$, the rate ratio is $\exp(0.20) \approx 1.22$, or about a
22% higher expected rate. A reference rate of 2 requests per 1,000 residents
would become about 2.44. In the fitted model, the density coefficient is
about $-0.165$, which corresponds to a rate ratio near 0.85: the fitted
request rate is about 15% lower for a one-standard-deviation increase in
density, conditional on this model. Population is an imperfect denominator
for illegal-parking reports: it does not measure vehicle activity, curb
supply, or reporting behavior. Neither this fitted association nor the
hypothetical calculation is a causal effect.

The Poisson model assumes that the conditional variance equals the
conditional mean. The Pearson chi-square statistic divided by residual
degrees of freedom gives a rough overdispersion check; values well above one
can indicate that the Poisson variation is too restrictive. Calculate this
diagnostic for the fitted model:


```{python}
poisson_fit.pearson_chi2 / poisson_fit.df_resid
```


The ratio is about 40.7, which indicates substantial overdispersion for this
specification. The Poisson fit therefore illustrates coefficient
interpretation, but it is not an adequate final model for these counts.
Its usual model-based standard errors and p-values do not support reliable
variable-significance claims under this variance mismatch.
Residual checks and the spatial structure of the areas also matter; a
negative binomial or another count model may be more appropriate.


## Check the Model


Model checks ask whether the chosen specification represents the observed
relationships adequately. They differ from test-set evaluation: a model can
fit the training records poorly, or fit them closely while predicting new
records poorly. Logistic regression does not assume normally distributed
errors or constant error variance as ordinary least squares does. Its
assumptions instead concern the conditional Bernoulli response and the
specified relationship between predictors and log odds. Residual and
influence diagnostics can reveal unusual records or lack of fit, but no
single diagnostic proves that a model is correct [@hosmer2013applied;
@pregibon1981logistic].


The current model makes several assumptions that can be checked only in
part:


- Each standardized area measure has a linear relationship with log odds.
- The model is additive, so the detail contrast is the same across boroughs
  unless an interaction is included.
- Sparse categories may produce unstable estimates.
- Repeated Census values mean that area-level patterns are supported by 176
  distinct ZCTAs rather than by the full request count.


Compare observed outcome rates with mean fitted probabilities across
boroughs and across ordered groups of each continuous predictor, retaining
the count in each group. Calibration is one check: predictions near 0.7
should correspond to an observed outcome rate near 0.7 among comparable
requests [@vancalster2019calibration].


The training-set summary below compares observed target rates with average
fitted probabilities by borough. A large discrepancy can flag a lack of fit
for a group, while close averages do not rule out errors for individual
requests or interactions hidden within a borough. This is an in-sample check
for the simple GLM, not an estimate of future prediction accuracy.


```{python}
from IPython.display import display

glm_diagnostics = glm_data[["borough"]].copy()
glm_diagnostics["observed"] = y_train
glm_diagnostics["fitted"] = glm_fit.fittedvalues
display(glm_diagnostics.groupby("borough").agg(
    requests=("observed", "size"),
    observed_rate=("observed", "mean"),
    mean_fitted_probability=("fitted", "mean"),
))

for variable in numeric_features:
    check = glm_data[[variable]].copy()
    check["observed"] = y_train
    check["fitted"] = glm_fit.fittedvalues
    check["quintile"] = pd.qcut(check[variable], 5, duplicates="drop")
    display(check.groupby("quintile", observed=True).agg(
        requests=("observed", "size"),
        observed_rate=("observed", "mean"),
        mean_fitted_probability=("fitted", "mean"),
    ))
```


The evaluation section checks calibration for a fitted model. A calibration
plot groups predictions into bins and compares each bin's mean predicted
probability with its observed fraction. The diagonal marks perfect
calibration; binning is a summary, so it can conceal variation within a bin.


## Evaluate Predictions


Evaluation asks how well the fitted model predicts requests it did not use
for estimation or tuning. A training score is optimistic because the model
has already adapted to those records. The reserved test set is used only
after model choice; repeatedly adjusting a model after inspecting its test
performance turns that set into another training resource and weakens the
evaluation. Here, even a clean random holdout supports only a limited claim:
it estimates performance for additional requests drawn under a similar
one-week data-generating process.


Prediction metrics depend on the outcome's scale. Numeric outcomes are
evaluated by comparing predicted values with observed values; classification
begins with class probabilities and applies a threshold to assign labels.
The same train-test separation applies to both tasks, but their metrics answer
different questions.


### Numeric outcomes


For the $n$ held-out observations, indexed by $i=1,\ldots,n$, let $y_i$
denote the observed outcome, $\hat{y}_i$ its prediction, and $\bar{y}$ the
mean of the observed outcomes. A residual is the observed value minus its
prediction. Three common scores summarize different aspects of these
residuals:


$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{MAE} &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|y_i - \hat{y}_i|, \\
\text{RMSE} &= \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}, \\
R^2 &= 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}
              {\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \bar{y})^2}.
\end{aligned}.
$$


Mean absolute error (MAE) reports a typical miss in the outcome's units.
Root mean squared error (RMSE) uses the same units but gives large errors
more influence because it squares them before averaging. The coefficient of
determination, $R^2$, compares squared prediction error with variation around
the observed mean; a test-set value can be negative when predictions are
worse than that reference [@scikitlearn2026metrics].


Recorded closure hours are numeric, so the held-out records also allow us to
compare simple duration baselines. The training mean is the constant
prediction that minimizes squared error; the training median minimizes
absolute error. This comparison shows how numeric prediction metrics work
without introducing a second fitted model.


```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score

duration_train = model_data.loc[X_train.index, "closure_hours"]
duration_test = model_data.loc[X_test.index, "closure_hours"]
duration_scores = {}
for name, value in {
    "Training mean": duration_train.mean(),
    "Training median": duration_train.median(),
}.items():
    prediction = pd.Series(value, index=duration_test.index)
    duration_scores[name] = {
        "MAE (hours)": mean_absolute_error(duration_test, prediction),
        "RMSE (hours)": mean_squared_error(
            duration_test, prediction
        ) ** 0.5,
        "R-squared": r2_score(duration_test, prediction),
    }
display(pd.DataFrame(duration_scores).T)
```


The training-median baseline has lower MAE (2.67 hours) than the training-mean
baseline (3.16 hours), while the mean baseline has lower RMSE (4.96 hours
versus 5.25 hours). The right-skewed closure-time distribution lets a few
long closures have a large effect on RMSE. Both $R^2$ values are near zero or
negative, so these constant forecasts capture little of the test-set
variation. They provide reference errors, not an evaluation of a
feature-based regression model.


### Binary outcomes


For binary classification, a model often estimates a probability and then
uses a threshold to assign one of two labels. The positive class is the
category of interest, and changing the threshold changes the predicted
labels and the resulting threshold-based scores.


The earlier coefficient tests concern associations in the unpenalized
training fit. The held-out scores below answer a different question: how
well do the fitted probabilities and labels predict requests outside that
fit? A small coefficient p-value alone cannot answer it.


A confusion matrix compares observed classes with the classes predicted at a
chosen threshold. For $n$ evaluated requests, its four cells count correct
and incorrect classifications.
A true positive (TP) is an actual positive predicted as positive; a false
negative (FN) is an actual positive predicted as negative. A false positive
(FP) is an actual negative predicted as positive; a true negative (TN) is an
actual negative predicted as negative. Rows below are actual classes and
columns are predicted classes, matching the convention used by scikit-learn
[@scikitlearn2026metrics].


| Actual class | Predicted positive | Predicted negative | Total |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Positive | TP | FN | TP + FN |
| Negative | FP | TN | FP + TN |
| Total | TP + FP | FN + TN | $n$ |

: General layout of a binary confusion matrix. {#tbl-model-confusion-matrix}


In this chapter's parking analysis, a positive is a request that closes in
under one hour, and a negative takes at least one hour. The illustrative
probability threshold is 0.5, so predicted
probabilities at or above 0.5 are classified as positive. The displayed
test-set counts use this rule and the layout in
@tbl-model-confusion-matrix.


Each metric uses a different margin or combination of cells. The numerator
and denominator make clear which errors a score counts:


| Quantity | Common names | Definition |
|:--|:--|:--|
| True positive rate | TPR, sensitivity, recall, hit rate, probability of detection | $\text{TP}/(\text{TP}+\text{FN})$: fraction of actual positives flagged |
| False negative rate | FNR, miss rate | $\text{FN}/(\text{TP}+\text{FN})$: fraction of actual positives missed |
| True negative rate | TNR, specificity, selectivity | $\text{TN}/(\text{TN}+\text{FP})$: fraction of actual negatives not flagged |
| False positive rate | FPR, fall-out, false alarm rate | $\text{FP}/(\text{TN}+\text{FP})$: fraction of actual negatives flagged |
| Positive predictive value | PPV, precision | $\text{TP}/(\text{TP}+\text{FP})$: fraction of flagged requests that are positive |
| False discovery rate | FDR | $\text{FP}/(\text{TP}+\text{FP})$: fraction of flagged requests that are negative |
| Negative predictive value | NPV | $\text{TN}/(\text{TN}+\text{FN})$: fraction of unflagged requests that are negative |
| False omission rate | FOR | $\text{FN}/(\text{TN}+\text{FN})$: fraction of unflagged requests that are positive |
| Accuracy | Overall accuracy, correct classification rate | $(\text{TP}+\text{TN})/(\text{TP}+\text{TN}+\text{FP}+\text{FN})$ |
| F1 score | F1 measure, F-score | $2\,\text{Precision}\,\text{Recall}/(\text{Precision}+\text{Recall})$ |


Different fields use different names for several of the same ratios:


- **TPR, sensitivity, and recall** all divide true positives by actual
  positives. They ask what fraction of requests that close in under an hour
  the model flagged.
- **PPV and precision** divide true positives by predicted positives. They
  ask what fraction of flagged requests closed in under an hour.
- **Specificity and TNR** measure the fraction of actual negatives not
  flagged; **FPR** is the fraction of actual negatives that were flagged.
- **F1** is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It does not account
  for true negatives.


The complementary pairs TPR/FNR, TNR/FPR, PPV/FDR, and NPV/FOR each sum to
one. For a positive weighting parameter $\beta$, the $F_\beta$ score makes
the precision-recall balance explicit:


$$
F_\beta = (1 + \beta^2)
\frac{\text{Precision}\,\text{Recall}}
     {\beta^2\,\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}.
$$


The familiar F1 score sets $\beta=1$. Values above one give more weight to
recall, while values below one give more weight to precision; the choice
should reflect the decision context rather than a universal preference
[@wikipediandevaluation; @scikitlearn2026metrics].


Accuracy is the fraction of correct labels and can hide poor performance on
one class when class frequencies differ. ROC AUC measures how well the model
ranks positive cases above negative cases across thresholds; 0.5 indicates
chance-level ranking and 1 indicates perfect ranking. AUC neither chooses a
threshold nor checks whether probabilities are accurate. Log loss evaluates
the probabilities themselves and penalizes confident errors. For $n$
evaluated observations indexed by $i=1,\ldots,n$, let $y_i\in\{0,1\}$
denote the observed outcome and $0<p_i<1$ its predicted probability. Log
loss is


$$
-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[y_i\log(p_i) + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\right].
$$


These measures answer different questions and none is universally best
[@scikitlearn2026metrics].


The threshold determines how missed short closures trade off
against unnecessary alerts. The data do not specify the costs of these errors, so
the example uses 0.5 only for illustration. A threshold selected for use
would be chosen with training or validation data, then evaluated once on the
held-out test set.


The baseline assigns every request the training-set target prevalence as
its probability and predicts the majority class. The model one-hot encodes
problem detail, borough, hour group, and day type; it standardizes the three
area measures and fits logistic regression. A small function creates a fresh
preprocessor for each model below, including the later cross-validation
examples. The function is available to the exercises in
`scripts/modeling_preprocessing.py`. Its encoder can handle a category in
the test set that was absent from training.


```{python}
from scripts.modeling_preprocessing import make_preprocessor
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
```


Keeping the transformer inside a pipeline makes the training step learn
categories and scaling only from training requests. Later, each validation
fold will learn them from its own training portion. The function also
accepts an additional transformer for the ZIP target-encoding comparison.


The baseline uses the training prevalence as the probability for every test
request. The logistic pipeline fits its preprocessing and coefficients on
training requests, then estimates a separate probability for each test
request. Neither model uses test outcomes during fitting.


```{python}
candidate_features = categorical_features + numeric_features
baseline = DummyClassifier(strategy="prior").fit(
    X_train[candidate_features], y_train
)
baseline_probability = baseline.predict_proba(X_test[candidate_features])[:, 1]

model = make_pipeline(
    make_preprocessor(categorical_features, numeric_features),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000),
)
model.fit(X_train[candidate_features], y_train)
test_probability = model.predict_proba(X_test[candidate_features])[:, 1]
```


At the illustrative 0.5 threshold, the confusion matrix shows the actual
outcomes in rows and predicted outcomes in columns. Displaying it before
the summary scores makes the errors behind those scores visible.


```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

confusion_table = pd.DataFrame(
    confusion_matrix(y_test, test_probability >= 0.5, labels=[1, 0]),
    index=["Actual under one hour", "Actual at least one hour"],
    columns=["Predicted under one hour", "Predicted at least one hour"],
)
confusion_table
```


Of the 1,120 requests that actually closed in under one hour, the model
flags 153 and misses 967. Among the 2,124 requests that took at least an
hour, it flags 112 and correctly leaves 2,012 unflagged. Thus, only 265
requests receive a positive label, even though 1,120 meet the target. The
following scores summarize these counts and also assess the probabilities
before any threshold is applied.


```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score, f1_score, log_loss, precision_score,
    recall_score, roc_auc_score,
)

def score_predictions(probability):
    predicted_class = probability >= 0.5
    return {
        "accuracy": accuracy_score(y_test, predicted_class),
        "ROC AUC": roc_auc_score(y_test, probability),
        "log loss": log_loss(y_test, probability),
        "TPR / recall": recall_score(y_test, predicted_class),
        "specificity": recall_score(y_test, predicted_class, pos_label=0),
        "precision": precision_score(
            y_test, predicted_class, zero_division=0
        ),
        "F1": f1_score(y_test, predicted_class),
    }
```


Accuracy, recall, specificity, precision, and F1 use the 0.5 labels.
ROC AUC and log loss use the probabilities directly, so changing only the
classification threshold would leave those two scores unchanged. The
same scoring function applies to the baseline and model probabilities.


```{python}
scores = pd.DataFrame({
    "Prevalence baseline": score_predictions(baseline_probability),
    "Request and Census-context logistic model": score_predictions(test_probability),
}).T
scores
```


The prevalence baseline predicts no short closures at a 0.5 threshold
because fewer than half of training requests have that outcome. It reaches
65.5% accuracy by labeling every request as taking at least an hour, but
its recall and F1 are zero. Its ROC AUC is 0.5 because its probability is
the same for every request.


The logistic model improves test accuracy only slightly, to 66.7%. Its
recall is 13.7% ($153/1{,}120$), so it misses most short closures at this
threshold. Its precision is 57.7% ($153/265$): among requests it flags as
closing under one hour, about 58 in 100 actually do. Its specificity is
94.7% ($2{,}012/2{,}124$), showing that it rarely flags requests that
take at least an hour. The F1 score of 0.221 reflects the low recall
despite moderate precision.


The model's ROC AUC of 0.618 exceeds the baseline's 0.5, so its
probabilities rank short closures above longer ones better than a constant
score does. Its log loss of 0.623 is also lower than the baseline's 0.644,
indicating a modest improvement in probability estimates. These results
show some predictive information, but they do not make 0.5 a suitable
decision threshold for every use.


The calibration plot compares predicted probabilities with the observed
fraction for the preliminary model. A probability estimate of 0.7 should
correspond to an outcome rate near 0.7 among comparable predictions
[@vancalster2019calibration]. The points group held-out requests into
quantile bins, so the display can hide variation within each group.


```{python}
#| label: fig-model-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Calibration of held-out probabilities for closures under one hour."
#| fig-format: svg
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve

observed_rate, mean_probability = calibration_curve(
    y_test, test_probability, n_bins=10, strategy="quantile"
)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.0))
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="0.5", linestyle="--", label="Perfect calibration")
ax.plot(mean_probability, observed_rate, marker="o", label="Request and Census context")
ax.set(xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1), xlabel="Mean predicted probability",
       ylabel="Observed fraction closing under one hour")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
```


In @fig-model-calibration, most bin averages lie near the diagonal. The
highest-probability tenth has a mean prediction of about 0.54 but an observed
short-closure fraction of about 0.59, suggesting some underprediction in
that group. This binned display checks the reported probabilities; it does
not determine any single request's true closure probability.


The ROC curve traces the true positive rate against the false positive rate
as the probability threshold changes. In the table above, TPR is also called
recall or sensitivity; FPR is one minus specificity. Each point represents
a different threshold, so the curve displays the trade-off between finding
more short closures and incorrectly flagging requests that take at least an
hour.
The area under this curve is the ROC AUC reported in the score table.


```{python}
#| label: fig-model-roc
#| fig-cap: "ROC curve for the preliminary request and Census-context model on held-out requests."
#| fig-format: svg
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve

false_positive_rate, true_positive_rate, _ = roc_curve(y_test, test_probability)
roc_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, test_probability)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.0))
ax.plot(
    false_positive_rate,
    true_positive_rate,
    label=f"Request and Census context (AUC = {roc_auc:.3f})",
)
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="0.5", linestyle="--", label="Chance ranking")
ax.set(xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1), xlabel="False positive rate (1 - specificity)",
       ylabel="True positive rate (sensitivity / recall)")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
```


This first comparison gives the model a common reference and an initial
held-out score. Its results are not the final model-selection result
because the regularization strength still needs to be chosen using training
data alone. A 0.5 classification threshold is convenient for illustration,
not a universal decision rule. A real alerting system would set a threshold
by considering the consequences of each kind of error with the people who
would use the predictions.


## Regularize a GLM {#sec-glm-regularization}


<!-- Instructor-source material: ids-s25/stats.qmd, LASSO Logistic Models
     (formulation, practical benefits, solution path, preprocessing), and
     ids-f25/09-classification.qmd, Tuning Regularized Logistic Models.
     Generalize the likelihood to GLMs; retain the simulated lasso path.
     Correct the likelihood scaling in the C-to-lambda conversion, fit
     scaling before computing the path, and keep preprocessing within CV. -->

The model has many coefficients because problem detail and borough are
one-hot encoded, and the later ZIP-label model adds a coefficient for each
observed area. Some categories are sparse, while the Census measures can be
correlated. An unpenalized fit can assign unstable, large coefficients to
these patterns and perform worse on new requests. Regularization limits
coefficient size to trade some training fit for more stable predictions.


### Penalized Likelihood

Generalized linear models estimate coefficients by maximizing a
distribution-specific likelihood. Let $\mathbf{y}$ be the response vector
for $n$ observations, $\mathbf{X}$ the predictor matrix, and
$\boldsymbol{\beta}=(\beta_0,\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_p)^\top$ the
coefficient vector, where $\beta_0$ is the intercept and $p$ is the
number of other coefficients. Let
$\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta};\mathbf{y},\mathbf{X})$ denote the **summed**
log-likelihood and $P(\boldsymbol{\beta})$ a penalty excluding the
intercept. A regularized GLM estimates the coefficients by


$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_\lambda
= \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
\left\{
-\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}; \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{X})
+ \lambda P(\boldsymbol{\beta})
\right\},
$$ {#eq-glm-penalized}

where $\lambda\geq 0$ is a tuning parameter controlling the strength of
regularization. A zero value gives the unpenalized objective; larger
values place greater weight on shrinking the coefficients. The likelihood
changes with the GLM response distribution and link, while the penalty
restricts the coefficients [@hastie2009elements].


The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (**lasso**) uses


$$
P(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|,
$$

where $j$ indexes the non-intercept coefficients. The absolute-value penalty
can shrink some coefficients exactly to zero, giving a sparse model
[@tibshirani1996regression]. Thus, lasso performs coefficient estimation
and variable selection together. It can be useful when many candidate
predictors are available, even when their number exceeds the number of
observations. Fewer nonzero coefficients can simplify interpretation, but
they do not establish which variables cause the outcome. With correlated
predictors, the selected variables can also change across samples.


Ridge uses the squared-coefficient penalty
$P(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2$ and
usually shrinks coefficients without setting them exactly to zero. These
are also called the $\ell_1$ and squared $\ell_2$ penalties,
respectively. Elastic net combines the lasso and ridge penalties
[@zou2005regularization]. Here we use lasso to make both shrinkage and
variable selection visible, following the logistic-model example below.
The earlier preliminary scikit-learn fit used its default ridge penalty;
penalty choice should be explicit when fitting the final model.


The same formulation applies to a Poisson GLM: replace the Bernoulli
log-likelihood with the Poisson log-likelihood and retain the chosen
coefficient penalty. Regularization does not correct overdispersion: a
Poisson GLM still assumes that conditional variance equals conditional
mean. Nor does it repair an inappropriate link or omitted predictors.


### Connecting the Formula to scikit-learn

Scikit-learn's `LogisticRegression` uses `C` to control regularization.
For unweighted observations, its objective can be written as


$$
-\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta};\mathbf{y},\mathbf{X})
+\frac{1}{C}P(\boldsymbol{\beta}),
$$

so comparison with @eq-glm-penalized gives $\lambda=1/C$. A smaller
`C` therefore means a larger $\lambda$ and stronger regularization;
a larger `C` permits larger coefficient estimates. This relationship
holds for both the lasso and ridge penalties just defined
[@scikitlearn2026logistic].


The likelihood convention matters. Dividing the entire objective by $n$
gives average negative log-likelihood plus $P(\boldsymbol{\beta})/(nC)$.
If $\lambda$ instead multiplies the penalty beside an **average** negative
log-likelihood, then $\lambda=1/(nC)$. These conventions describe the
same fit after converting the parameter; the examples here use the summed
likelihood convention. The conversion is specific to `LogisticRegression`;
other GLM implementations may use different controls.


Numeric predictors should be standardized before penalized fitting because
the penalty acts on coefficient size. Changing a predictor's units changes
the coefficient needed to describe the same relationship and therefore
changes its penalty. Standardization gives each numeric predictor mean zero
and standard deviation one in the fitting data. As in the earlier pipeline,
category encoding and scaling must be learned from training records alone.


### The Lasso Solution Path

A solution path shows how coefficient estimates change as $\lambda$
varies. We retain the simulated example with 100 observations, 20 candidate
features, and two informative features. The generator's default also creates
two redundant features from the informative features; the remaining features
are noise. A selected feature need not be one of the two original informative
features when correlated alternatives are available.


```{python}
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

path_X, path_y = make_classification(
    n_samples=100, n_features=20, n_informative=2, random_state=2026
)
path_X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(path_X)
```


The fixed seed 2026 makes this simulation reproducible. All observations
are used to illustrate fitting; this path is not a prediction-performance
evaluation. Standardizing before constructing the grid ensures that its
scale matches the features actually supplied to the model.


For lasso logistic regression, the intercept-only fitted probability is
$\bar y=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_i$, the observed event rate. The largest
absolute slope of its log-likelihood at zero coefficients gives


$$
\lambda_{\max}
=\max_{1\leq j\leq p}
\left|\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{ij}(y_i-\bar y)\right|,
$$

where $z_{ij}$ is standardized feature $j$ for observation $i$.
At or above this value, zero is a solution for every non-intercept
coefficient. We fit 100 candidates from $\lambda_{\max}$ down to
$0.01\lambda_{\max}$, equally spaced on a logarithmic scale.


```{python}
lambda_max = np.abs(path_X.T @ (path_y - path_y.mean())).max()
lambda_grid = np.geomspace(lambda_max, 0.01 * lambda_max, 100)
```


The `saga` solver supports lasso and leaves the intercept unpenalized.
With the class environment's scikit-learn version, `l1_ratio=1` specifies
lasso; `l1_ratio=0` specifies ridge. Each model below uses `C=1/lam`
to match the summed-likelihood definition of $\lambda$.


```{python}
path_rows = []
for lam in lambda_grid:
    path_model = LogisticRegression(
        l1_ratio=1, solver="saga", C=1 / lam,
        max_iter=5000, tol=1e-6, random_state=2026
    )
    path_model.fit(path_X, path_y)
    path_rows.append(path_model.coef_.ravel())
```


We reshape the estimates so that each curve represents one coefficient.
The intercept is excluded because it is not penalized.


```{python}
path = pd.DataFrame(path_rows, columns=[f"x{j + 1}" for j in range(20)])
path["lambda"] = lambda_grid
path = path.melt(id_vars="lambda", var_name="feature", value_name="coef")
```


The horizontal axis is logarithmic, so equal distances correspond to equal
ratios of penalty strength. Moving right increases $\lambda$ and pulls
more coefficients to zero. The figure illustrates shrinkage; selecting
$\lambda$ requires a separate validation criterion.


```{python}
#| label: fig-model-lasso-path
#| fig-format: svg
#| fig-cap: "Lasso logistic coefficient paths for 20 standardized simulated features. Moving right increases the penalty strength; the intercept is not shown."
#| fig-alt: "Twenty coefficient curves approach zero as lambda increases on a logarithmic axis. At the strongest penalty, all non-intercept coefficients are zero to numerical tolerance."
import plotnine as gg

gg.options.figure_format = "svg"

(
    gg.ggplot(path, gg.aes("lambda", "coef", group="feature"))
    + gg.geom_hline(yintercept=0, color="gray", linetype="dashed")
    + gg.geom_line(color="#0072B2", alpha=0.65)
    + gg.scale_x_log10()
    + gg.labs(x=r"Penalty strength $\lambda$", y="Coefficient estimate")
    + gg.theme(figure_size=(7, 4))
)
```


## Select the Tuning Parameter {#sec-glm-tuning}


A tuning parameter controls the fitting procedure rather than being
estimated as a regression coefficient. Too much regularization can remove
useful predictors; too little can retain patterns specific to the training
sample. We select its value by comparing predictions on validation records,
using the same criterion for every candidate. The coefficient path helps
explain what the parameter does, while cross-validation assesses its
predictive consequences.


Cross-validation uses training data alone. Within each fold, the pipeline
learns its scaling, category encoding, and model coefficients from the
fold's fitting records. For a candidate setting $h$, let $K$ be the number
of folds, $V_k$ the validation records in fold $k$, and $|V_k|$ their
number, for $k=1,\ldots,K$. Let
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-k}(h)$ denote the coefficients fitted
without fold $k$, and let $\mathbf{y}_{V_k}$ and $\mathbf{X}_{V_k}$
be its validation responses and predictor matrix. The fold's average
negative log-likelihood and the mean cross-validation loss are


$$
\begin{aligned}
L_k(h) &=-\frac{1}{|V_k|}
\ell\!\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-k}(h);
\mathbf{y}_{V_k},\mathbf{X}_{V_k}\right),\\
\operatorname{CV}(h)&=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}L_k(h).
\end{aligned}
$$


The validation likelihood evaluates predictions without adding the fitting
penalty. For Bernoulli responses, this average negative log-likelihood is
log loss, introduced in the prediction-metrics section. Other criteria
include ROC AUC, F1, and accuracy; the criterion should match the intended
use and be chosen before inspecting test results. We use log loss because
the goal is to estimate closure probabilities rather than optimize a
particular classification threshold.


The selected candidate has the smallest mean validation loss and is
refitted on the complete training set. The separate test set remains
untouched until selection is complete. Reporting the best validation score
as final performance can be optimistic because that score also guided the
selection [@scikitlearn2026crossvalidation; @varma2006bias]. The more
general model-selection discussion continues in @sec-machine-learning.


### Tune the Request Models

The comparison separates measured area context from a postal-code lookup.
All four models use the same training and test requests. Each includes
problem detail, borough, hour group, and day type. One model uses those
request features; a second adds three ACS-derived area measures; a third adds
the incident ZIP label as a categorical identifier; and a fourth uses a
smoothed target encoding of that label. All four use lasso.
Five-fold stratified cross-validation selects `C` by log loss. Standardization and one-hot encoding are
inside the pipeline so each fold learns its preprocessing from its own
training portion. The ZIP-label model is a predictive benchmark for areas
already represented in the data; its coefficient for a ZIP label does not
explain what neighborhood feature may relate to closure time.


```{python}
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=2026)
candidate_C = {"logisticregression__C": [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10]}
```


The candidate grid covers four orders of magnitude in `C`. It is specified
explicitly, not inferred automatically from the data. If validation loss
keeps improving at a grid boundary, extend that boundary using training
data before evaluating the test set. The search holds `C` fixed across
folds and during refitting; its summed-likelihood penalty is therefore
$\lambda=1/C$ throughout.


The helper creates a fresh preprocessing pipeline for each feature set.
`GridSearchCV` fits and scores every candidate within the five folds and
refits the best candidate on all training records. Scikit-learn maximizes
scores, so `neg_log_loss` returns the negative of the loss we want to
minimize. The double underscore in `logisticregression__C` names the
`C` parameter of the pipeline's logistic-regression step.


```{python}
def tune_logistic(categorical, numeric):
    pipeline = make_pipeline(
        make_preprocessor(categorical, numeric),
        LogisticRegression(
            l1_ratio=1, solver="saga", max_iter=5000, random_state=2026
        ),
    )
    search = GridSearchCV(
        pipeline,
        candidate_C,
        scoring="neg_log_loss",
        cv=cv,
        refit=True,
    )
    features = categorical + numeric
    search.fit(X_train[features], y_train)
    return search
```


The helper places standardization and one-hot encoding inside each
cross-validation fold, so validation records do not determine their own
preprocessing. It uses log loss to select `C` and returns the fitted search.
The first comparisons assess request features, area context, and a ZIP-label
identifier.


```{python}

zip_identifier_features = categorical_features + ["incident_zip"]
request_features_search = tune_logistic(
    categorical_features, []
)
census_search = tune_logistic(
    categorical_features, numeric_features
)
zip_id_search = tune_logistic(
    zip_identifier_features, []
)
```


The validation curve makes the selection visible rather than reporting only
the winning `C`. We extract each candidate's mean validation log loss for
the Census-context model and mark the selected value. All values in this
plot come from training folds.


```{python}
cv_result = pd.DataFrame(census_search.cv_results_)
cv_loss = pd.DataFrame({
    "C": cv_result["param_logisticregression__C"].astype(float),
    "log_loss": -cv_result["mean_test_score"],
})
selected_C = census_search.best_params_["logisticregression__C"]
```


```{python}
#| label: fig-model-lasso-cv
#| fig-format: svg
#| fig-cap: "Mean five-fold validation log loss for the lasso model with Census context. The dashed line marks the selected C; smaller losses are better."
#| fig-alt: "Validation log loss is plotted against C on a logarithmic axis. A vertical dashed line identifies the candidate with the smallest mean loss."
(
    gg.ggplot(cv_loss, gg.aes("C", "log_loss"))
    + gg.geom_line(color="#0072B2")
    + gg.geom_point(color="#0072B2")
    + gg.geom_vline(xintercept=selected_C, linetype="dashed")
    + gg.scale_x_log10()
    + gg.labs(x=r"$C=1/\lambda$", y="Mean validation log loss")
    + gg.theme(figure_size=(7, 4))
)
```


### Tune the ZIP Encoding

One-hot encoding gives each ZIP label its own coefficient, which can be
unstable when some labels have few requests. Smoothed target encoding offers
another representation: it replaces a label with an estimate of its
under-one-hour closure rate, then shrinks that estimate toward the overall rate.
For ZIP label $j$, a common estimate is


$$
  \widetilde{p}_j =
  \frac{s_j + \alpha \bar{p}}{n_j + \alpha},
$$


where $s_j$ is the number of requests closing in under an hour with
label $j$, $n_j$ is its number of requests, $\bar{p}$ is the overall training-set rate, and
$\alpha$ controls shrinkage. Larger values of $\alpha$ pull area
estimates more strongly toward the overall rate. This empirical Bayes idea
is useful for categories with different sample sizes
[@micci-barreca2001preprocessing; @pargent2022regularized]. Since the
encoding uses the outcome, fitting it on each row's own outcome would leak
information into the training data. The encoder below cross-fits the
training values within each training fold; for the held-out test set, it
uses category rates estimated from the full training set
[@scikitlearn2026targetencoder].


The smoothing value and logistic penalty strength are selected together by
cross-validation. The first part of the pipeline constructs the predictors,
including a target encoder for the ZIP label.


```{python}
from sklearn.preprocessing import TargetEncoder

zip_target_pipeline = make_pipeline(
    make_preprocessor(
        categorical_features,
        extra=[(
            "zip_target",
            TargetEncoder(
                target_type="binary",
                cv=StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=2026),
            ),
            ["incident_zip"],
        )],
    ),
    LogisticRegression(
        l1_ratio=1, solver="saga", max_iter=5000, random_state=2026
    ),
)
```


The grid now has 15 combinations: three smoothing strengths and five `C`
values. The outer folds evaluate the whole pipeline. Inside each outer
fitting fold, the target encoder uses its own inner folds to keep a row's
outcome out of its encoded value. Both layers use training data alone.


```{python}
zip_target_search = GridSearchCV(
    zip_target_pipeline,
    {
        "columntransformer__zip_target__smooth": [1, 10, 100],
        "logisticregression__C": [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10],
    },
    scoring="neg_log_loss",
    cv=cv,
    refit=True,
)
zip_target_features = categorical_features + ["incident_zip"]
_ = zip_target_search.fit(X_train[zip_target_features], y_train)
```


### Evaluate the Selected Models

All tuning is complete before the following test predictions are made.
The four prespecified comparisons use the same held-out requests; their
scores describe this comparison, rather than supplying a further tuning
criterion.


```{python}
request_features_probability = request_features_search.predict_proba(
    X_test[categorical_features]
)[:, 1]
census_probability = census_search.predict_proba(
    X_test[categorical_features + numeric_features]
)[:, 1]
zip_id_probability = zip_id_search.predict_proba(
    X_test[zip_identifier_features]
)[:, 1]
zip_target_probability = zip_target_search.predict_proba(
    X_test[zip_target_features]
)[:, 1]
```


The first table compares held-out prediction scores using the same scoring
function for all four models. The following table reports their tuning
settings separately.

```{python}
comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    "Request details and timing": score_predictions(request_features_probability),
    "Census area context": score_predictions(census_probability),
    "ZIP label identifier": score_predictions(zip_id_probability),
    "ZIP target encoding": score_predictions(zip_target_probability),
}).T
comparison.round(4)
```


The tuning summary records each selected `C`, its equivalent $\lambda$
for the summed likelihood, and its validation loss. The target-encoding
model also reports its selected smoothing strength.


```{python}
comparison["C"] = [
    request_features_search.best_params_["logisticregression__C"],
    census_search.best_params_["logisticregression__C"],
    zip_id_search.best_params_["logisticregression__C"],
    zip_target_search.best_params_["logisticregression__C"],
]
comparison["lambda"] = 1 / comparison["C"]
comparison["cv_log_loss"] = [
    -request_features_search.best_score_,
    -census_search.best_score_,
    -zip_id_search.best_score_,
    -zip_target_search.best_score_,
]
comparison["zip_smooth"] = [
    None,
    None,
    None,
    zip_target_search.best_params_["columntransformer__zip_target__smooth"],
]
comparison[["C", "lambda", "cv_log_loss", "zip_smooth"]].round(4)
```


For this split, adding the Census measures changes test ROC AUC from about
0.601 to 0.620 and log loss from 0.630 to 0.622. The improvement is modest,
but it indicates that the supplied area attributes add some predictive
information beyond problem detail, borough, hour group, and day type in this
test design. The ZIP-label model scores higher, with ROC AUC about 0.687 and
log loss 0.594.
Because the same ZCTAs occur in training and test sets, this score reflects
area-specific prediction for locations represented in training. It neither
identifies a cause nor demonstrates transfer to a new ZCTA or a later week.


Smoothed target encoding gives a similar test ROC AUC of about 0.690 and
log loss of 0.593, with the cross-validation procedure selecting a smoothing
value of 10. Three test requests have ZIP labels absent from the training
set; the encoder assigns those labels the overall training rate. This
comparison shows that a compact, partially pooled encoding can retain much
of the ZIP-specific predictive signal in this split. It does not establish
that ZIP-level outcome rates will transfer to future requests, and its
learned category values should not be interpreted as neighborhood causes.


The Census estimates offer a more interpretable area-level question than
the ZIP label, but they do not measure the mechanisms that directly govern
parking or request processing. Population density is residents per square
mile, not curb or parking-space density. Household vehicle availability is
not ownership, registration, vehicle activity, or parking location, and
median household income does not describe an individual requester. These
ACS measures repeat across requests in the same ZCTA and carry sampling
uncertainty; the vehicle share's uncertainty has not been propagated. Only
176 ZCTAs contribute independent area contexts in this analysis. Direct
measures of curb regulations, parking supply, vehicle activity, or precinct
workload would be more informative for those processes. Any resource-
allocation use would also require a separate review of measurement, fairness,
and consequences for affected neighborhoods.


Regularization controls model complexity but does not replace diagnosis.
The selected penalty can stabilize estimates while leaving omitted
variables, measurement error, unfair performance differences, and domain
changes unresolved. Area-level predictors also require validation that
respects their shared geography when the intended use concerns new areas.
The model's intended use and validation design must therefore be considered
together.


## Exercises {.unnumbered}

The exercises use the same merged request-ZCTA table as the chapter examples.
Run `python scripts/build_parking_with_zcta.py` from the repository root to
write `data/parking_requests_with_zcta.parquet`. The script calls
`load_parking_requests()` and then `attach_zcta_context()`, just as the
example above does, and saves the merged table. Read the file with
`pd.read_parquet()`. It retains continuous `closure_hours` and unmatched
requests but has no binary outcome. Treat recorded closure time as a proxy
for handling time, not as a direct measure of officer response.

::: {#exr-model-check}
Prepare and fit a logistic model for closures lasting at least five hours.
Use problem detail, borough, creation-time group, business-day status,
population density, median household income, and household vehicle
availability as predictors. Derive the two timing features from `created_at`
using the definitions in this chapter. Import `make_preprocessor` from
`scripts.modeling_preprocessing` to encode the four categorical predictors
and standardize the three area measures inside the fitting pipeline.

a. Construct the complete-case data. Report the eligible count and
   exclusions for missing closure time, unmatched ZCTAs, and missing area
   estimates.
b. Create a binary outcome from `closure_hours` that equals one for durations
   of at least five hours and zero otherwise. Report its count and proportion.
c. Compare the five-hour cutoff with the closure-time distribution. Explain
   why the cutoff is an analytical choice rather than an agency standard.
d. Identify which predictors are available at request creation. Make a
   stratified training and test split before fitting.
e. Tune logistic regression's `C` on the training set using stratified
   cross-validation and mean log loss. Report the candidate grid, its scores,
   and the selected value.
:::

::: {#exr-model-logistic-evaluate}
Assess the model selected in @exr-model-check on held-out requests.

a. Refit the selected model on all training requests. Compare its test ROC
   AUC and log loss with a prevalence baseline.
b. At a stated probability threshold, report TPR, precision, F1, and the
   confusion matrix for the test requests.
c. Make a test-set calibration plot. Describe one pattern it reveals about
   the predicted probabilities.
d. Compare test performance by borough, creation-time group, and business-
   day status, reporting group counts with each score.
e. State one limitation of the day-type comparison for this week.
:::

::: {#exr-model-logistic-interpret}
Interpret fitted logistic models for the five-hour outcome. Use the selected
regularized model for parts a–c and a separate unpenalized GLM for parts d–f.

a. Choose one standardized area predictor. Report its coefficient and odds
   ratio, and interpret a one-standard-deviation increase with other
   predictors held fixed.
b. Apply that odds ratio to reference probabilities of 0.20 and 0.50.
   Explain why the two probability changes differ.
c. Choose one problem-detail coefficient. Identify its reference category,
   and state the outcome and predictor contrast.
d. Fit an unpenalized logistic GLM on the training requests with standard
   errors clustered by ZCTA.
e. Report a joint test for creation-time group and a 95% odds-ratio interval
   for one area predictor. Interpret both results.
f. Explain why these tests do not establish practical importance, held-out
   predictive value, or a causal effect, and why their p-values do not apply
   to the selected regularized model.
:::

::: {#exr-model-zip}
Examine what a ZIP-label model adds to prediction.

a. Fit a model that treats ZIP as a categorical identifier, using the same
   training and test requests and tuning procedure as @exr-model-check. Add
   `incident_zip` to the categorical inputs of `make_preprocessor`.
   Compare its held-out performance with the Census-context model.
b. State what this benchmark can and cannot show about unfamiliar ZCTAs.
c. For the Census-context model, report ROC AUC under request-random and
   ZCTA-grouped validation.
d. State which prediction setting each validation design evaluates.
:::

::: {#exr-model-count}
Fit and assess a Poisson model for request counts by NYC ZCTA.

a. Construct one count per ZCTA from matched requests, starting from the
   complete ZCTA lookup to retain zero counts. Report areas excluded for
   missing population or density.
b. Explain why the ZCTA, rather than the request, is the observational unit.
c. Fit a Poisson model with population in thousands as an offset and
   standardized population density as a predictor. Report the density
   coefficient and rate ratio.
d. Interpret the rate ratio for a one-standard-deviation increase in density.
e. Explain one limitation of population as an exposure measure.
f. Fit the same model without the offset. Compare fitted coefficients and
   predicted counts, and explain how the prediction question changes.
g. Calculate the Pearson chi-square statistic divided by residual degrees
   of freedom. Interpret it and name one model or predictor to investigate
   if the Poisson variance assumption is inadequate.
h. Explain whether the model's usual p-value for density is reliable in
   light of this dispersion check.
:::

::: {#exr-model-poisson-regularized}
Investigate regularization for the ZCTA count model. Use population in
thousands as an offset and population density, median household income,
and household vehicle availability as predictors. Interpret associations
without causal claims.

a. Report any additional ZCTAs excluded for missing predictors.
b. Split ZCTAs into training and test sets. Standardize predictors within
   each training fold so validation ZCTAs do not determine their own scaling.
c. Tune an $L_2$ penalty over a stated grid using cross-validation within
   the training set and mean Poisson deviance. Report the candidate scores
   and selected penalty.
d. Refit the selected regularized model and the unpenalized model on the
   training ZCTAs. Compare their test-set Poisson deviances.
e. Compare the models' coefficients and describe how the penalty changes
   their estimates.
f. Explain why regularization does not resolve overdispersion.
g. Explain how dependence among nearby ZCTAs limits a random area-level
